To summarise, the typological evidence suggests that number and gender tend to be realised cumulatively. When they are expressed separately, it appears that gender is likely to appear closest to the stem; and in systems where the reverse order exists, genderclosest orders are also found. However, the data on separative morphology here are notably sparse. Both trends nonetheless have factored into formal theories of gender and number, where several distinct proposals have been made for how these features are formalised and mentally represented.

1.3 Theories of Gender and Number Representation, and Their Impact on Morpheme Ordering

Formal linguistic theories differ substantially in terms of how gender is argued to be represented, and in how it interacts with number. These theories have been designed (although not uniquely) to account for the kind of cross-linguistic data discussed above, and make different predictions about the kinds of inferences human learners might make when learning gender and number systems.

In relation to our object of study, the main source of diver-gence across these different theories is whether gender projects together with number in nominal morphology. (10) DP D NumP Num [PL] nP / NP n / / 0 √ / N GENDER here in bundling models GENDER here (i.e., in n, or N) in split models

In one well-known class of theories, gender is represented-i.e., projected in the morphosyntax-separately from number. Following Fuchs et al. (2015), we call these split models (see ( 10)). Intuitively, gender may seem to be an inherent property of a nominal head; in most cases, nouns have only one fixed gender, and gender can be assigned arbitrarily. This implies that gender may project in the syntax together with the nominal head. Indeed, there are proposals which argue that gender features are part of the lexical entry for a given noun. While these accounts capture the close relationship between nouns and gender, additional mechanisms are needed to capture systematic relationships between noun semantics (e.g., sex or animacy) and gender, and to deal with variable gender (i.e., stems that can be feminine or masculine depending on the properties of the referent). To account for these phenomena, lexicalist theories of gender often differentiate nouns that are specified for gender from those that are unspecified (Alexiadou, 2004; Carstens, 2010; Harris, 1991; Roca, 1989). 8 Alternative theories which project the noun and gender features together (separate from number) use Distributed Morphology (Kihm et al., 2005; Lowenstamm, 2008; Kramer, 2015). These accounts argue that nominal heads themselves have a more complex structure, with stems that are category neutral and a nominalising functional head n, where gender is located (see ( 10)). Thus gender is within the nominal head and plays a role in turning a stem (i.e., √ in ( 10)) into a noun in a way that can be sensitive to semantics when necessary (see, e.g., Kihm et al., 2005; Lowenstamm, 2008; Kramer, 2015). There are also some split models which propose a distinction between variable-and fixed-gender nouns. For example, fixed gender might be projected within nP (n phrase) , and variable gender outside the nominal, within an intermediate gender phrase (GenP) lower than the number phrase (NumP) (see Panagiotidis, 2018, for additional discussion of how this differs from a lexicalist model).

While split models (including lexicalist models) represent gender and number in an inherently asymmetrical way where gender is more local to the nominal head than number, an alternative model locates gender together with number in the NumP (i.e., see schematic representation in (10); Ritter, 1993; Carstens, 2003; Giurgea, 2008). 9 Following Fuchs et al. (2015), we call this the bundling model. Like split models, some bundling models treat fixed and variable gender distinctly. For example, some bundling models argue that gender projects with number for variable (semantic) gender marking, but not for fixed gender, where it is considered to project with the nominal head (Carminati, 2005; De Vincenzi, 1999).

Assuming that the affix order reflects structural relations in morphosyntactic composition (e.g., Embick, 2010; Bobaljik, 2012; Baker, 1985), split and bundling models capture different cross-linguistic tendencies regarding the interaction between gender and number morphology. If gender and number are bundled together and thus project together (as the bundling model proposes), this predicts cumulative exponence, which is indeed extremely common. However, as discussed above, there are cases where gender and number are expressed as separate affixes, and in those cases, gender morphology typically appears closer to the stem than number. Moreover, there are many instances in which gender and number seem to act separately, even if they can be expressed cumulatively in other contexts. For example, Romance languages such as Italian and Spanish-which have both number and gender morphology-have verbal agreement with the subject noun in number but not gender. These phenomena (amongst others) suggest that at the very least gender and number can project separately. This possibility is captured by split models. Even though these models may differ with regard to whether the representation of gender is an inherent part of the noun or a projecting head immediately dominating it, they all predict that gender should be placed closer to the stem than number in cases where the exponence of gender and number is non-cumulative, a tendency tentatively supported by the cross-linguistic data discussed above. By contrast, bundling models make no clear predictions about order (i.e., without further ad hoc ordering mechanisms forcing number to linearise outside of gender; e.g., Ritter, 1993).

1.4 Other Explanations of Gender and Number Morpheme Ordering

The theories discussed above make predictions (or not) about order on the basis of structural morphosyntactic representations of gender and number. However, there are other explanations of morpheme order that are potentially relevant for gender. For example, Greenberg (1963) introduced the notion of proximity hierarchies for nominal morphology, essentially dictating which morphemes are closer to the stem than others. He speculated that this was "related to degrees of logical and psychological remoteness" from the stem (Greenberg, 1963, , p. 103). In his proposal, proximity hierarchies were also related to other implicational hierarchies relevant to inflectional categories, for example, regarding markedness or syncretism. For case and number morphology, Greenberg (1963) placed number higher on the proximity hierarchy (i.e., closer to the stem) than case based on a set of observations: (i) number almost always appears closer to the stem than case cross-linguistically (Universal 39; Greenberg, 1963), (ii) many languages with systematic number marking lack case but not vice versa, and (iii) case is more likely to be neutralised within a given number value than number is to be neutralised within a given case value (Baerman et al., 2005; Corbett, 2000 Corbett, , 1991)). Building on these notions, Bybee (1985) developed the relevance hierarchy.

Under her proposal, morphemes which are more relevant to the stem will be placed closer to it. For case and number morphology, she suggests that number appears closer to the stem because it directly modifies the entity referred to by the noun (i.e., it is very relevant to the noun). By contrast, the case morpheme signals an external relationship between the entity and some event (i.e., it is less relevant to the noun stem), thus it appears further away from the stem. Neither Greenberg (1963)'s notion of proximity hierarchies nor Bybee (1985)'s relevance hierarchy have been explicitly applied to other nominal inflectional features. However, for gender and number morphology, the general line of argumentation would likely be less straightforward. Number should be placed higher in the proximity hierarchy than gender on the basis of markedness or syncretism (e.g., there are many languages with the number category and without gender, but the reverse is rare; and gender is more likely to be the neutralised feature within a given number in pronouns and other agreement targets; Baerman et al., 2005; Corbett, 1991 Corbett, , 2000)). However, as discussed above, gender is likely to be linearly closer to the stem when it appears separate from number (Di Garbo, 2014; Kramer, 2015), which would require gender to be higher on the proximity scale. Gender might be considered higher on the related relevance hierarchy as well, given that it can reflect highly specific semantic features of the stem, like sex and animacy.

More recently, alternative explanations of morpheme order focus on the role of distributional cues like the frequency with which stems and affixes (co-)occur. The general idea is that stem+affix pairs that co-occur more frequently will be more likely to be ordered closer to one another (e.g., Ryan, 2010; Hay, 2001; Hay and Plag, 2004). In some cases, the relevant notion is degree of dependency, or strength of association, which can be quantified using mutual information between stem and affix. Hahn et al. (2021) show that this is a good predictor of the relative order of verbal affixes in a number of different languages. Rathi et al. (2022) further argue that this same measure can predict patterns of fusion between morphemes (i.e., the degree to which formatives are phonologically intertwined with their host). This is reminiscent of accounts of word order arguing that mutual information can predict linear distance between head and dependents (Futrell et al., 2015 (Futrell et al., , 2020;; Hahn et al., 2020; Culbertson et al., 2020). Distributional statistics like these have the potential to make predictions about gender and number. Notably, stems and gender affixes are likely to cooccur very frequently, more so than stems and number markers. For example, in Spanish, where number and gender are not cumulative, singular is zero-marked while gender values are overtly marked or cued with the same forms across singular and plural nouns. In this case, the co-occurrence frequency (and mutual information) is likely to be higher between a stem and a gender morpheme than between a stem and a number morpheme. 10

1.5 Experimental Evidence for Preferences in Morpheme Ordering

The pervasiveness of cumulative exponence of gender-number morphology and the scarcity of documented separative exponence makes it difficult to assess whether there is support for theories which predict clear ordering preferences between these two inflectional categories. Moreover, the frequent coexistence of fixed and variable gender within the same system of gender marking makes it difficult to explore potential differences in their linguis-tic representations. However, even if natural language data were plentiful and typological regularities were robustly quantified, cross-linguistic tendencies are not necessarily directly linked to individual-level mental representations or biases. Tendencies could reflect historical contingencies, cognition-external pathways of change, or even common distributional properties of the linguistic input that reflect communicative needs rather than learning biases or mental representations. For instance, as we have summarised in the previous section, some studies have shown that co-occurrence statistics among stems and morphemes, rather than any abstract representations of their structure, may determine morpheme order and morphological fusion both within and across languages (Hahn et al., 2021 (Hahn et al., , 2022;; Rathi et al., 2022; Hay, 2001; Hay and Plag, 2004).

Experimental research offers a way to test these different theories, and in particular to uncover evidence for representations or biases that shape gender and number systems. For example, if particular ways of ordering morphemes are preferred by learners in carefully controlled experiments, this can provide evidence for specific theories or representations. It also provides a potential link between human cognitive biases and typology: individual learners' preferences can be amplified as languages are transmitted from generation to generation (Thompson et al., 2016; Kirby et al., 2015). Saldana et al. (2021) used a series of artificial language learning experimental studies to show that English-and Japanese-speaking participants' inferences about number and case morphemes follow the cross-linguistic trend in having number closer to a noun stem than case. This held even though co-occurrence statistics among stems and different affixes were kept constant. Saldana et al. (2021) argue that this ordering preference therefore likely reflects differences in the kinds of meanings conveyed by these two types of morphemes (e.g., following Bybee, 1985; Culbertson et al., 2020).

Here, we use a similar experimental design to probe the biases of language learners with regards to the relative order of gender and number morphology. We train participants on miniature nominal systems with separative number and gender morphology, but holding out any evidence about the relative order of these morphemes in the language. By holding distributional information-that is, co-occurrence frequencies between stems and morphemes-constant, we can isolate the impact of the features themselves. For example, we can directly test whether learners' biases more closely align with split models of gender and number, or with bundling models. As discussed above, split models-which are the most commonly assumed-predict that participants should express gender closer to the noun than number. By contrast, if gender and number are bundled together, we wouldn't predict any particular ordering preference to be more likely than another (without further constraints). If these hypothesised structural representations in fact play no role in speakers' minds, and order is fully determined by distributional information accessible to the learner during acquisition, then equally, we should see no preference for one order over the other when input frequencies are controlled.

In the experiments described below, we also explore whether learners' ordering preferences are consistent regardless of experience with gender systems in their first language (L1), and whether preferences differ when participants are taught fixed and variable gender systems. As mentioned above, in some formal theories variable and fixed gender have been argued to behave in different ways (with variable gender projecting higher, either with number or with its own head Carminati, 2005; De Vincenzi, 1999; Panagiotidis, 2018), which could potentially affect the strength of any ordering preferences-e.g., they might be weaker for variable gender systems than for fixed gender systems.

2 Study 1: Ordering Preferences for Gender and Number Morphemes across Populations

In the first set of experiments, we train adult English-, Italian-, and Kîîtharaka-speaking participants on miniature nominal paradigms with separative exponence of gender and number morphology. We focus on nominal gender marking (and not on agreement targets), and gender assignment is exclusively (and not only partly) based on the semantics of the nouns. Gender assignment can be based either on animacy and fixed (i.e., stems denote either animate or inanimate entities), or based on sex and variable (i.e., stems denote only sexdifferentiable entities, and they can be either male or female). We refer to these conditions as animacy-based and sex-based, respectively. Participants' training input indicates whether gender and number affixes generally precede or follow the noun stem (i.e., they are either all prefixes or all suffixes), but crucially participants are not given any examples in which overt gender and number affixes co-occur on the same noun. Participants thus know whether the novel language is prefixal or suffixal but they have no evidence indicating in which way gender and number affixes are ordered when they appear together within the same noun. At test, they are asked to produce an order for these held-out examples. These productions will reveal the inferences learners make regarding the relative order of gender and number morphology, in the absence of any evidence in the input linguistic system.

We compare speakers' preferences across different linguistic populations in order to assess whether substantially different experience with gender systems in their L1 affects the results. English marks (plural) number on nouns, but does not mark gender. 11 Thus English-speaking participants have no evidence from their L1 (either for sex-based or for animacy-based systems) of how inflectional morphemes of gender and number should be ordered relative to one another. They do, however, have evidence of derivational gender morphemes being placed closer to the root than (inflectional) number (e.g., lion-ess-(e)s), which in the absence of any other gender linguistic representation could make participants place sex-based gender markers closer to the stem because they treat them as derivational morphology. The animacy-based system we use here is quite distinct from this.

In contrast to English, Italian-speaking participants' L1 marks both gender and number, but cumulatively (see ( 3)-(4) above). The system can be characterised as sexbased, with both variable and fixed sub-systems. If Italian speakers also prefer to place number in the periphery, it will not be because they are only familiar with inflectional affixes with number information alone (see Saldana et al., 2021, for related evidence). Their knowledge of gender also makes it less likely that they would fall back on experience with derivational morphology to determine order.

Finally, Kîîtharaka-speaking participants' L1 is like Italian in featuring cumulative gender and number exponence. However, like other Bantu languages, it is prefixing and its gender system can be described as containing an animacy-based semantic core. It has a relatively large number of classes, typically treated as singular-plural pairs, with classes partly determined by semantics. The most obviously inflectional semantic feature is human vs. non-human (e.g., CL1 and CL2 nouns are exclusively human, singular and plural, respectively; Kanampiu et al., 2025b). Some Kîîtharaka class markers have been analysed as derivational (since they can be used to express diminutive, augmentative, pejorative meanings). However, unlike English and Italian, Kîîtharaka does not have any derivational morphology that expresses sex differences, and derivational uses of gender morphemes still cumulatively express number.

To preview, the order participants infer across all three linguistic populations indicates a clear preference for placing gender closest to the noun, in accordance with a representation in which gender is more closely tied to the noun than number is. This is straightforwardly predicted by split models (e.g., Picallo, 1991; Harris, 1991; Kramer, 2015) which argue that gender and number are projected separately, with gender either forming part of the nominal projection or immediately dominating it. By contrast, to account for these results, bundling models would require ad hoc ordering mechanisms (e.g., Ritter, 1993). We also find that Italian speakers are slightly more likely to produce the reverse orders for variable-gender systems than for fixed-gender systems. This is not the case for English speakers, where we find no difference between gender systems. These results therefore expand the range of behavioural evidence for the role of cognitive representations in determining morpheme order, and further suggest a possible difference between the representations of gender across variable-and fixed-gender systems (consistent with the models proposed in , e.g., Carminati, 2005; De Vincenzi, 1999) that is worth exploring further in future work.

2.1 Materials and Methods

Our experiments use an extrapolation design to test participants' preferences for gender and number morpheme ordering on nouns (following Saldana et al., 2021). Participants were trained on a subset of a nominal system with two gender classes and two number values (singular and plural). Across all conditions, only one gender class is overtly marked via affixation, the other is not; and only one number value is overtly marked via affixation, the other is not. The system is thus designed such that only some forms involve affixes of both gender and number. Crucially, these forms are held out during training, but participants are asked to infer them during testing. During training, participants therefore learn only how single morphemes are ordered relative to the noun stem. At test, they must therefore infer the relative order of the two. They can either place the gender morpheme closer to the noun stem than the number morpheme, or vice versa.

Experiments with English and Italian speakers were designed using a 2 × 2 between-subjects factorial design where we manipulated the position of affixes (either all suffixes or all prefixes) and the type of gender system (either animacy-based or sex-based).

In one condition, the gender systems mark perceived biological sex of non-human animals with sexual dimorphism. For example, the stem alone is used to refer to the animal with female characteristics (FEM), and the stem together with an overt gender affix is used when the same denoted animal shows male characteristics (MASC). We refer to this condition as sex-based, but it also corresponds to what we have called a variable system above, since the same stem encoding a single meaning (type of animal) can be inflected for both genders (here via an overt affix vs zero-marking). The other condition, which we call animacybased, is closer to what we have called a fixed gender system. In this condition, gender distinguishes between animate (ANIM) and inanimate (INANIM) entities and the denoted entity type cannot be both ANIM and INANIM. Stems denoting animates are marked with an affix, and stems denoting inanimates are zero-marked. 12.

We want to control for stem-affix co-occurrence statistics equally across conditions and we need to share the stem forms across classes in fixed animacy-based systems as well as in variable sex-based systems; the only way to do this is by constructing homophonous stems across classes in the animacy-based condition. The correspondence between the animate and inanimate meanings of two homophonous stems is therefore arbitrary in the fixed animacy-based systems (see table 1). Having shared stem forms in both sex-based and animacy-based conditions allows us to match co-occurrence frequencies (and mutual information) across all stem-affix combinations. Thus learners exposed to both variable-and fixed-gender systems must make inferences about order in the absence of distributional information.

The design used for Kîîtharaka speakers diverges from this. After piloting, we determined that the above systems were not readily learned by our Kîîtharaka population (described in detail below), therefore we went with a simpler system that is more naturallanguage-like. 13 First, in this system, gender classes convey a more salient animacy distinction for the target population, that is, between humans and inanimate objects. Second, stems are not shared across gender classes, but are unique-as they are mostly in natural language. Note then that here the co-occurrence frequencies of stem+affix combinations are not matched; the same stem form can only appear in one gender class, and thus stems overtly marked for gender are always marked for gender (and never appear with zero marking). We discuss the implications of this difference in light of the results below.

2.1.1 Artificial Lexicon

Participants were trained on a language with a small lexicon of four (English and Italian speakers) or eight (Kîîtharaka speakers) stem forms 14 , and two affixes, one expressing number (plural) and the other expressing gender (masculine or animate for the sex-based or animacy-based condition, respectively). Across all conditions, singular was always unmarked and plural was marked; similarly, one gender value was always marked with an affix and the other is not. For English and Italian speakers, in sex-based conditions MASC was overtly marked and FEM unmarked (i.e., we ensure that the gender marker is not as straightforwardly mapped to the derivational feminine gender affix in the speakers' L1); in animacy-based systems, ANIM was marked and INANIM unmarked. For Kîîtharaka speak-ers INANIM was always unmarked as well.

The two affixes marking gender and number values were randomly chosen for each participant from the set {gu, sa, vi} (English), {gu, sa, di} (Italian), or {ke, bu, ra} (Kîîtharaka). 15 Gender and number affixes were attached to stems, with the relative order of affixes and nouns (prefixing or suffixing) determined by the condition. For Englishand Italian-speaking participants, we tested both suffixing and prefixing, for Kîîtharakaspeaking participants we tested only prefixing. 16 Examples of a full lexicon for each gender system type and each language population are shown in table 1.

During training phases (described below), participants saw three kinds of nominal forms in the language: the stem alone (singular, unmarked class), gender-marked stems (singular, marked class), and number-marked stems (plural, unmarked class). Crucially, forms in which both number and gender overt morphology would be required-i.e., plural, gender-marked class-were held out. As noted above, for English-and Italian-speaking participants, each of the four stems is used equally frequently in both gender classes, and with both numbers, therefore no co-occurrence statistics that differentiate stem+number from stem+gender combinations are present during training. In Kîîtharaka speakers, because stems are not shared across classes, marked gender class stems always occurred with the gender marker. Thus co-occurrence statistics would indicate to participants that stem+gender combinations are more frequent.

2.1.2 Experimental Procedure

The experiments were programmed using jsPsych (De Leeuw, 2015) and displayed in participants' browser windows. Before starting the experiment proper, participants were told they would learn how to describe simple pictures in a new language. The training phase was divided into three sub-phases: exposure, picture-matching, and recall. In the critical testing phase, we asked participants to produce word forms which were held out during the training.

During exposure, participants saw images along with orthographically presented nouns using a stem alone, or a stem with a single affix (either number or gender). More specifically, they were trained on three different types of inflected forms (see table 1): the stem alone (G1. SG, where SG → / 0 and G1 → / 0), gender-marked stems (G2. SG, where SG → / 0 and G2 → affix), and number-marked stems (G1. PL, where PL → affix and G1 → / 0). Participants saw each stem in each of these three forms five times, for a total of 60 trials (randomly ordered for each participant).

In the picture-matching phase, participants saw two images and a form and were ask to click the image corresponding to the form. As in the exposure phase, forms featured either a stem alone, or a stem with a single morpheme (either number or gender). The foil image for each trial was either the wrong gender, or the wrong number. Participants saw each stem with each pairing of correct and foil three times, for a total of 48 matching trials (randomly ordered for each participant).

In the recall phase, participants were tested on the forms they had been trained on so far (i.e., G1. SG, G1. PL, and G2. SG). In each trial, they saw an image and were asked

Full feedback was provided. Participants saw each stem inflected for G1. SG, G1. PL, and G2. SG three times (36 trials in total, randomly ordered for each participant).

In the critical testing phase participants were tested on the form-meaning mappings which were held out during training, i.e., those corresponding to forms inflected for G2. PL. At the end of the experiment, participants completed a survey in which they provided descriptions for each of the number and gender affixes in the artificial language.

2.1.3 Participants

English-and Italian-speaking participants were recruited through Prolific (http://www.prolific.co) and paid 10 GBP/h for participation in the study, which took approximately 12 minutes. We used Prolific screening criteria to include native English-and Italian-speaking participants who were raised monolingual and whose primary language was still their L1 at the time of the study. 17 Kîîtharaka-speaking participants were recruited via local contacts in Kenya (specifically, in Tharaka-Nithi county, the main region where the language is spoken). Participants were largely students at Tharaka University, and most were multilingual speakers of Swahili, English, or both. Participants were sent a link to the experiment, and after completing the experiment, they were paid 400 KES.

As per our preregistration, participants who got less than 75% correct on recall trials in the training phase were excluded (N = 9 both for English and for Italian, and N = 1 for Kîîtharaka). For English and Italian speakers, a total of 80 participants' data were analysed for each language (20 in each condition of our 2x2 factorial design); for Kîîtharaka speakers, a total of 28 participants' data was analysed (all belonging to the same condition, as described above). 18

2.1.4 Data Analysis

For each population tested, we used R's brms (Bürkner, 2018) library as an interface to Stan (Carpenter et al., 2017) to fit a mixed-effects Bayesian binomial model predicting participants' production of gender-closest order (stem-G2-PL if suffixing or PL-G2-stem if prefixing). Our dependent variable was participants' responses for each of the critical test trials (coded as 1 if gender-closest, and 0 if number-closest). For English and Italian, we included fixed effects of affix position (suffixing vs prefixing, treatment-coded) and gender system (sex-based vs animacy-based, treatment-coded), as well as their interaction.

As random effects, we included intercepts for participants as well as stems. We set the same Student-t prior on all effects and intercepts (DF = 6, µ = 0, σ = 1.5); for random effects' standard deviations, we set a half-Cauchy prior with a scale parameter 1. The model for the experiment with Kîîtharaka speakers was intercept-only (as we only have one condition); the random effects structure and priors were set as in the previous models.

We fitted two further models, one comparing the experiments with English and Italian speakers and the other comparing the prefix animacy-based conditions across all three linguistic populations (Kîîtharaka, English, and Italian). In the former model we used the same model structure as the one described above for English and Italian with the added fixed effect of language group (English vs. Italian) and an interaction term. In the latter model, we used the same model as for the experiment with Kîîtharaka speakers alone but instead of an intercept-only model, we add the effect of linguistic population (Kîîtharaka, English, and Italian). We used Kîîtharaka as the baseline, since the artificial system was designed to mirror closely that of Kîîtharaka-with the only difference being that morphology was separative-and the co-occurrence statistics in the experiment with Kîîtharaka speakers were much stronger between stems and gender affixes than between stems and number affixes.

2.1.5 Transparency and Openness

All data and analyses reported are available at https://osf.io/hmt7b. The preregistered hypothesis, design, and analysis plan can be found at https://osf.io/z2c9m (for English) and https://osf.io/un8yx (for Italian). We preregistered English and Italian language groups as different experiments, and the latter as a replication of the former with a different language group. 19 The Kîîtharaka experiment was not preregistered.

2.1.6 Ethics

All studies in this article have been approved by the Ethics Committee of the School of Philosophy at the University of Zurich (Ref. No. 22.10.12) and the PPLS Research Ethics Committee at the University of Edinburgh (Ref. No. 423-2122/2).

2.2 Results

On the basis of our preregistered hypothesis, and in line with the commonly assumed split models, we predicted that participants would prefer to place gender morphology closer to the stem than number morphology in systems where both gender and number affixes are separate and both are placed before or after the stem. In the experiments with English and Italian speakers, we further explore whether participants are equally likely to produce gender-closest orders across animacy-based (fixed) and sex-based (variable) gender systems. Recall that in variable-gender systems, lexical stems map to a single meaning and are inflected for different gender feature values (as in the sex-based system in our experiments); in fixed-gender systems, lexical stems are either shared idiosyncratically across classes (as in the animacy-based systems in our English and Italian experiments) or are not shared at all (as in the animacy-based system in our Kîîtharaka experiment). Average proportion of responses with gender-closest order among English-(A), Italian-speaking (B), and Kîîtharaka-speaking participants (C) in Study 1, by affix position and gender system type. Coloured dots represent participants' individual scores; black dots represent the model's predicted mean accuracy scores and the error bars represent the model's predicted 90% credible intervals (CI). Dashed lines represent the chance level.

Figure 3 shows average proportions of responses with gender-closest orders in the critical trials for participants in the populations and conditions we tested. A visual inspection suggests that our results are consistent with the preregistered predictions: participants infer gender-closest orders (i.e., stem-G2-PL or PL-G2-stem), regardless of affix position, type of gender system, or participant population.

The model results confirm this. For English-speaking participants, the intercept provides strong evidence that English speakers prefer to produce gender-closest as opposed to number-closest orders in animacy-based prefixal systems ( β = 6.348, 90%CI = [4.779, 8.189], P( β > 0) = 1). This preference is not weaker in other conditions (sex-based vs. animacy-based prefixal: β = -0.857, 90%CI = [-2.426, 0.661], P( β < 0) = 0.821; interaction with suffixal systems: β = -0.300, 90%CI = [-1.969, 1.304], P( β < 0) = 0.618; animacy-based suffixal vs. prefixal: β = -0.721, 90%CI = [-2.179, 0.686], P( β < 0) = 0.802).

For Italian-speaking participants, the model also confirms notably above-chance production of gender-closest orders in the reference animacy-based prefixal condition ( β = 7.235, 90%CI = [5.373, 9.434], P( β > 0) = 1), which is equally strong for animacybased suffixal systems ( β = -0.550, 90%CI = [-2.217, 1.087], P( β > 0) = 0.709). We find evidence (although weak, P( β < 0) < 0.95) suggesting that Italian speakers are slightly less likely to produce gender-closest orders in sex-based systems (sex-based vs. animacy-based prefixal: β = -1.628, 90%CI = [-3.489, 0.094], P( β < 0) = 0.941; interaction with suffixal order: β = -0.523, 90%CI = [-2.416, 1.316], P( β < 0) = 0.676). We observed this same tendency with the English data, however,in that case the evidence was not decisive (P( β < 0) ≈ 0.8). However, a further model combining the data from English and Italian speakers, reveals the same effect of system type in the data from English speakers (sex-based < animacy-based) and no difference between the English the Italian speakers' data (sex-based vs. animacy-based prefixal with English speakers: β = -1.315, 90%CI = [-2.899, 0.210], P( β < 0) = 0.923; interaction with language group: β = -0.887, 90%CI = [-2.606, 0.773], P( β < 0) = 0.808). Note, however, that the evidence is weak across models (P( β < 0) < 0.95) and it could be driven by the stark homogeneity in our data, where almost all participants choose gender-closest orders categorically and a few outliers could easily drive differences across conditions.

Finally, and unsurprisingly, for Kîîtharaka-speaking participants, the model intercept provides very strong evidence for a preference to produce gender-closest as opposed to number-closest orders ( β = 4.623, 90%CI = [2.590, 6.751], P( β > 0) = 0.993). Interestingly, however, a further model comparing the accuracy in the animacy-based prefixal condition across language groups suggests that this preference for gender-closest orders is comparable (Italian vs. Kîîtharaka: β = 0.674, 90%CI = [-0.870, 2.312], P( β > 0) = 0.758; English vs. Kîîtharaka: β = 0.670, 90%CI = [-0.878, 2.373], P( β > 0) = 0.753), thus suggesting that the preference for gender-closest orders is not aided by very strong cooccurrence statistics (as found in the system used in the experiment with Kîîtharaka speakers).

2.3 Discussion

The experiments in Study 1 tested whether language learners with different L1s would infer that a novel gender morpheme should be ordered closer to the noun stem than a novel number morpheme. As described above, the precise systems participants were taught differed across populations. Importantly, the training input for English and Italian speakers was designed so that no co-occurrence statistics would lead learners to prefer one order over the other (suggested as a mechanism for ordering preferences in, e.g., Hahn et al., 2022). In other words, stems occurred equally frequently with the gender and number morphemes. This was not the case for Kîîtharaka-speakings participants, for whom we used a simplified language that resembled typical natural language gender systems: stems marked with an overt gender affix always occurred with that affix. Nevertheless, our results confirm a strong preference for ordering gender morphemes closer to the stem than number morphemes across all populations. The fact that the preference was equally strong across these populations suggests that higher co-occurrence frequencies are not necessary to skew participants' performance in favour of gender-closest order. The similar strength of preference regardless of L1 experience with gender further suggests that the preferences are not driven by knowledge of the relative order of derivational and inflectional affixes. While this could potentially explain English speakers' placement of gender closer to the stem-i.e., if their lack of experience with gender leads them to treat this morpheme as derivational-it is not likely to explain the results for Italian or Kîîtharaka speakers. Italian speakers arguably had no reason to treat the systems they were trained on here as anything other than akin to gender in their language. Kîîtharaka does not have derivational morphology that can be separated from number.

The results are also unlikely to be explained by differences in participants' ability to learn or correctly interpret the meanings of gender and number morphemes. Training phase accuracy scores (in picture-matching and recall tests) for English and Italian speakers were uniformly high. The proportions of correct interpretations of the affixes in the post-experimental survey were also high. Proportions of English and Italian participants reporting the correct interpretations for gender morphemes were between 70% and 75% in animacy-based systems, and between 85% and 100% in sex-based systems; 85%-100% of participants provided correct interpretations for number morphemes. Most Kîîtharakaspeaking participants (93%) also provided correct interpretations for number morphology in the post-experiment questionnaire; however, only 46% of participants provided correct interpretations for the gender morphology, suggesting that the gender markers in this experiment-which, unlike in the other experiments, were attached to stems that were never seen in isolation-were potentially harder to process as separate morphology and that they were most likely processed either as part of the stem or as singular markers when contrasted to the straightforwardly interpretable plural morphology. Indeed, most participants who provided an alternative description for gender markers interpreted them as singular markers (N = 9/15, 60%).

It is also worth noting that participants inferred the predicted order regardless of whether the system was prefixal or suffixal, confirming that this preference is not about the sequential order of the morpheme-i.e., which one is linearly first absolutely-but about which morpheme should be closer to the noun stem. We also found that the preference towards number-closest orders is consistent across sex-based variable gender, and animacybased fixed gender systems. This suggests that the interpretation of gender across the board leads to a gender-first derivation-i.e., gender combines morphosyntactically with the stem first-separate from number.

Moreover, we generally found that the type of gender system-fixed or variabledid not substantially alter the strength of the preference for gender-closest orders. That said, we did find a slight difference in the likelihood of producing the reversed number-closest order across gender system types: both English and Italian speakers tended to produce this reverse order slightly more often in sex-based variable systems. This might be taken to suggest that gender morphemes are more likely to be treated as separate from the stem when the stem is used to derive related entities (e.g., male vs. female of a given animal as in our sex-based condition). This is potentially in line with theories that posit that gender is derived with the noun stem in fixed systems and with number in variable systems (e.g., De Vincenzi, 1999). However, given the strength of the overall preference, we cannot rule out the possibility that our sample size is insufficient to assert the difference found across fixed and variable gender, and that datapoints driving the effect might be outliers (see figure 3).

Altogether, these results suggest that speakers' mental representations of gender and number impact ordering preferences. In particular, these representations are such that gender is consistently placed closer to the noun stem than number morphology is. This overwhelming preference cannot be straightforwardly explained by theories which bundle together gender and number features, such as the one proposed for Romance languages in (Ritter, 1993). Nor can it be explained by distributional information alone (Hahn et al., 2022). Rather, this preference mirrors a trend in the typology of separative gender-number systems captured by theories that argue for a representation of gender together with (or closest to) the noun (Harris, 1991; Alexiadou, 2004; Mel'čuk, 2013; Kramer, 2015 Kramer, , 2016b)). Of course, the pervasiveness of cumulative gender-number marking in noun affixes still requires explanation. Our findings could point toward alternative mechanisms, for example the grammaticalisation of gender systems. However, it is worth noting that we only test fully semantically-based gender classification systems. We return to this in the general discussion.

Before that, however, we return to the observation that the tendency to place the expression of gender or gender-conditioned information closer to the noun is also found in double plurals (Di Garbo, 2014; Kramer, 2016a; Acquaviva, 2008). In the examples provided above in section 1.1 for Kinshasa Lingala (see 8), an affix which expresses gender and number cumulatively is placed closer to the stem than a general number affix (which does not express any gender feature). Kramer (2016a) describes a similar tendency for the double plurals found in Amharic (Afro-Asiatic). In Amharic there is a general plural marker which can be used with all stems (referred to as regular plural in Kramer, 2016a), and other plural markers which can only be used only with a restricted set of stems (referred to as irregular plurals). Both types of plural markers can co-occur on the same nominal form simultaneously, and in these doubly marked plural nouns, the more restricted number marker is always closer to the stem than the general number marker (for further evidence in Breton and Somali, see also Acquaviva, 2008; Lecarme, 2002; Alexiadou, 2024). This recurrent double plural pattern suggests that number expressions might not all be equivalently represented. In particular, we might expect that general number morphemes are represented as hierarchically higher than gender-specific number morphemes (i.e., those restricted to a class of stems). In fact, in many proposals, the gender-specific plurals are considered to be lexical and projecting in n as gender in (9), and general plurals are considered to be grammatical plurals projecting in NumP (Acquaviva, 2008; Kramer, 2016a; Alexiadou, 2004 Alexiadou, , 2024, ;, ; cf. Mathieu, 2014). Assuming that linear proximity mirrors local structural rela-tionships between morphemes (Bobaljik, 2012; Embick, 2010; Baker, 1985), this would explain why they are realised closer to the stem cross-linguistically.

Interestingly, the system Kîîtharaka-speaking participants learned in Study 1 could be somewhat parallel to this. Given their L1 experience-i.e., extensive cumulative marking of gender and number-these participants may have learned that the gender affix was a cumulative singular-human class morpheme-indeed, many interpreted it as a singular marker-and that the number affix was a cumulative plural-inanimate class morpheme. If so, then essentially, the test phase requires them to disregard the class information in the plural morpheme and use it as a general plural at test. This is of course, highly speculative. In the following section we present an experiment explicitly testing ordering preferences of general and gender-specific plural affixes in double plural constructions.

This experiment serves two purposes. First, it allows us to test whether plurals carrying or being conditioned by the expression of gender are consistently placed closer to the stem by language learners. If so, this would provide support for the idea that any morpheme carrying gender information should be closer to the stem than any morpheme not carrying such information. This in turn would suggest that distinct representations of number can exist. Second, since both morphemes will express plural (which is more straightforwardly an inflectional category in participants' L1), this experiment will allow us to confirm even more strongly that the results of Study 1 are not driven only by a bias to place derivational (or more derivational-like) morphology closer to the stem than inflectional morphology.

3 Study 2: Ordering Biases for General and Gender-specific Number Morphemes

Following Study 1, in Study 2 we use an artificial language learning paradigm to test whether the inferences learners make about the order of gender-specific (here, conditioned by gender class information) and general (here, independent of gender class information) number morphology support the idea that these two types of number morphemes are represented distinctly. In particular, gender-specific plurals are hypothesised to be lower in the hierarchy or derived earlier than general plurals, which are higher in the hierarchy (Kramer, 2016a; Acquaviva, 2008; Alexiadou, 2024). 20 As in the previous experiments, here we control for any effects of input statistics on participants' ordering preferences. In this case, we explicitly compare order preferences for stems where co-occurrence statistics are balanced, and those which are not. This is explained in more detail below.

3.1 Materials and Methods

As in the set of experiments in Study 1 above, here we use an extrapolation design. We train native English speakers on a subset of a nominal system with two gender classes (human and non-human) and two number values (singular and plural). Plurals are overtly marked in this system, and they can be marked with a productive general plural affix or a plural affix that is restricted to a particular gender class. During testing, we ask participants to produce double plurals for the nouns they have been trained on, that is, to use both general and gender-specific plural affixes together.

The experiment features a 2 × 2 between-subjects factorial design where we manip-
