Each of the two gender-specific plural affixes occurs only with nouns in one gender class; the general plural affix occurs with (a subset of) nouns in both gender classes. Stems that occur with both plural morphemes are referred to as unrestricted stems; stems that occur with only gender-specific plural morphemes are referred to as restricted stems.

ulate the type of affixation (suffixing or prefixing) and the order of the training blocks of the different plural markers (general or gender-specific first). Participants were exposed to three blocks of training in total, as described in detail below.

3.1.1 Artificial Lexicon

Participants were trained on a language with a small lexicon of 8 stems, and 3 affixes. Stems belonged to one of two gender classes, the first containing human referents, the second containing inanimate referents (the same meanings used in the Kîîtharaka experiment in Study 1). There were four stems in each gender class. All three morphemes expressed plural meaning, but one (the general plural) co-occurs with stems belonging to any gender class, and two (the gender-specific plurals) co-occur only with stems in a given gender class. All plural affixes are attached to stems, both either as prefixes or suffixes, depending on the condition (randomly assigned for each participant at the beginning of the experiment).

An example of the artificial lexicon participants are trained on is provided in table 2. During training, participants see half of the stems for each class with both general and gender-specific plurals (unrestricted stems) and the other half only with the gender-specific plurals (restricted stems). This allows us to (1) show participants that there is a plural that is not dependent on gender while the other two are, (2) match the frequency of all plural morphemes, and (3) maintain the same point-wise mutual information across affixes and a subset of stems. The latter is discussed further below.

3.1.2 Experimental Procedure

The experiment was programmed using jsPsych (De Leeuw, 2015) and displayed in each participant's browser window. Before starting the experiment proper, participants were told they would learn "how to describe objects and people" in a new language. The training phase was divided into three sub-phases: exposure, picture-matching, and recall. In the final critical testing phase, we ask participants to produce doubly marked plurals and thus add the two affixes (general and gender-specific) to the stems.

During the exposure phase, participants saw images along with orthographicallypresented descriptions using a stem alone, or a stem with a single plural affix (either general or gender-specific). In the first block, they were exposed to bare stems, which expressed singular meanings. Participants saw each bare stem twice (i.e., twice for each of the four human stems and twice for each of the four inanimate stems, 16 trials in total, randomly ordered for each participant). In two subsequent blocks they were taught general and gender-specific plurals separately. The order of the general and gender-specific plural training blocks was determined randomly for each participant. Before the first plural training block, participants were told they would be learning"how to form plurals, that is, how to refer to a group of objects or people". Before the second plural training block, participants were told that this was not the only way to refer to groups of objects or people, and that there was another way which they will proceed to learn. In the gender-specific plural block, they saw each of the eight stems four times with the corresponding plural marker (total of 32 trials, randomly ordered for each participant). In the general plural block, they saw only four stems (two assigned to the human gender class and two to the inanimate, see section 3.1.1 above), four times each (total of 16 trials, randomly ordered for each participant).

Importantly, this training regime entails that point-wise mutual information (pmi) between any combination of plural affix (general or gender-specific) and unrestricted stem (those that appear both with both types of plurals) is exactly the same (pmi = 0.585). This is important because it means participants could not use co-occurrence statistics in the input to inform their decision about whether to order gender-specific or general plurals closer to these stem. For restricted stems (which only appear with a gender-specific plural morpheme) the pmi between stems and affixes is higher (pmi = 1.585). Thus in principle participants could use this kind of distributional asymmetry to guess the order of plural morphemes. In the test phase (described below) participants were asked to form double plurals with both unrestricted and restricted stems; they do so for unrestricted stems first.

In the next part of the training, the picture matching phase, participants saw two images and a description (using a stem alone or a stem and one plural affix, either general or gender-specific) and had to click the corresponding image. The foil image for each trial was either the wrong gender or the wrong number. Participants saw each stem twice in the singular, twice with the gender-specific plural, and each restricted stem was seen twice in the general plural (40 trials total, 16 singular, 16 gender-specific plural, 8 general plural, randomly ordered for each participant). Co-occurrence statistics were held constant as described for the previous exposure phase.

In the recall phase, participants were tested on the forms they had been trained on. In each trial, they saw an image and had to construct the corresponding form by clicking buttons. The buttons always included the correct stem and two affixes. For plural trials, the two affix buttons were the target affix and a foil, the incorrect gender-specific plural affix. For singular trials, the two affix buttons (both foils) were the general plural affix and the gender-specific plural affix matching the stem. Trials were constructed so that the cooccurrence statistics were maintained as in the previous phases. The general plural was never a foil affix, only a target. Therefore, no explicit evidence is provided in this phase that restricted stems cannot be pluralised with general plurals. Participants saw each of the bare stems or stem+affix combinations they were trained on three times (total of 60 trials, i.e., 24 singular, 24 gender-specific plurals, and 12 general plurals, randomly ordered for each participant).

In the critical testing phase, participants were asked to produce double plurals. Participants were reminded that they "have learned that there are two ways of forming plurals" and were told that "speakers of this language can actually use both together". On each trial, participants saw a plural image and had to construct a doubly-marked form by clicking buttons. The buttons on each trial included the stem, the correct gender-specific plural affix (i.e., the one that matches the gender class of the stem) and the general plural affix. Participants had to use all three buttons and could not submit their answer until they did. No other feedback was provided.

In the first block of testing, participants only saw unrestricted stems, that is, stems which appeared with both types of plurals during training. They were asked to produce double plurals three times for each unrestricted stem (total of 12 trials, randomly ordered for each participant). Recall that for these items, the frequency of all single affix-stem combinations during training is the same (pmi = 0.585) and there is thus no evidence that one or the other plural affix is more closely associated with a stem based on co-occurrence statistics.

In the second block of testing, participants saw restricted stems. They were asked to produce double plurals three times for each restricted stem (total of 12 trials, randomly ordered for each participant). For these items, there is a higher point-wise mutual information between the gender-specific plural affixes and stems (pmi = 1.585) compared to general plurals and stems. There was no break between this second block and the first block if testing.

3.1.3 Participants

English-speaking participants were recruited through Prolific as in our previous experiments and paid 10 GBP/h for participation in the study, which took approximately 15 minutes. We used Prolific screening criteria to include only native English-speaking participants who were raised monolingual and whose primary language was still their first language at the time of the study. As per our preregistration, participants whose accuracy was lower than 90% in the last block of the single morpheme production phase during training were excluded. We also excluded participants who did not produce affixes as ei-ther both suffixes or both prefixes during testing. After exclusions (N =35), a total of 120 participants' data was analysed (30 in each condition of our 2x2 factorial design).

3.1.4 Data Analysis

We ran Bayesian logistic regression models to test whether participants were more likely to produce gender-specific plural morphemes (containing gender information) closer to the stems than the general plural morpheme (without gender information). The model's fixed effects were affix position (treatment coded, suffixal vs prefixal), training block order (dummy coded, irregular first = 0, and regular first = 1), and stem type (treatment coded, with restricted stems vs. unrestricted stems), and their interactions. As random effects, we included intercepts for participant and gender class (human or non-human), and byparticipant slopes for the effects of stem type.

3.1.5 Transparency and Openness

All data and analyses reported are available at https://osf.io/hmt7b. The preregistered hypothesis, design and analysis plan can be found at https://osf.io/h4sgk. 21

3.2 Results

Based on our preregistered hypothesis, we predicted that (1) participants would prefer to place gender-specific plurals closer to the stem than general plurals, that (2) they would do so independently of the affix position and the input co-occurrence statistics, but (3) that this preference would potentially be stronger with restricted stems than with unrestricted stems as the dependency between gender-specific plurals and restricted stems was stronger.

A visual inspection of the results, shown in figure 4, suggests that our predictions are generally met. Overall, participants show a preference to place gender-specific plurals closer to the stem than general plurals, and this effect is stronger for those stems which appeared with only a gender-specific plural during training (i.e., restricted stems). The model results confirm these observations. The intercept estimates provide strong evidence in favour of a preference for ordering the gender-specific plural closer to unrestricted stems in the prefixed condition when gender-specific plurals are taught first ( β = 2.203, 90%CI = [0.695, 3.456], P( β > 0) = 0.977). We did not find robust evidence for an effect of training order (general first: β = -0.593, 90%CI = [-1.823, 0.582], P( β < 0) = 0.791; general first and suffix: β = -1.003, 90%CI = [-2.556, 0.501], P( β < 0) = 0.863) or affix type ( β = -0.552, 90%CI = [-1.776, 0.637], P( β < 0) = 0.775); this suggests that the preference for placing gender-specific plurals closer to unrestricted stems applies comparably across conditions.

The model results further suggest that the preference for placing gender-specific plurals closer to stems increases for restricted stems as predicted ( β = 1.637, 90%CI = [0.479, 2.929], SE = 0.745, P( β > 0) = 0.993). This effect is stronger in suffix conditions ( β = 1.077, 90%CI = [-0.262, 2.451], SE = 0.829, P( β > 0) = 0.907), and is potentially driven by the greater difference found in the suffix condition when the general plural is Average proportion of responses with gender-specific plural ordered closest to the stem among English-speaking participants in Study 2, by affix type (suffix or prefix), training block order (genderspecific or general plural first) and stem type (unrestricted or restricted). Coloured dots represent participants' individual scores; black dots represent the model's predicted mean accuracy scores and the error bars represent the model's predicted 90% credible intervals. Dashed lines represent the chance level.

taught first. This is also shown in figure 4: the difference between restricted and unrestricted stems is greatest in the condition with suffixes and general plural training first. Here, participants have a strong preference for gender-specific number closest for restricted stems but they have no preference for either order with unrestricted stems. We nevertheless do not find strong support for these observations in our model, only a mild tendency (general first and suffix: β = -1.003, 90%CI = [-2.556, 0.501], SE = 0.934, P( β < 0) = 0.863; general first, suffix, and restricted stems: β = -0.648, 90%CI = [-2.293, 0.954], P( β < 0) = 0.746). We will discuss possible explanations for this asymmetry across conditions in section 4.2.

3.3 Discussion

In Study 2, we explored whether participants' preference for ordering gender information closer to the stem than number would extend to a system in which the morpheme encoding gender information expressed number. In this system, plural meaning could be expressed using either one marker alone or both markers together. Participants tended to place gender-specific number markers (which appeared only with the nouns assigned to a specific gender class) closer to the stem than general number markers (which could appear with stems of either class). We also found some evidence for an influence of co-occurrence statistics: the preference for gender-closest order was greater for restricted stems. However, it is also worth noting that, despite being explicitly told that morphemes expressed plural meaning, in our post-experiment questionnaire, participants varied in whether they explicitly interpreted both morphemes as having a plural meaning: 64% of participants explicitly identified plural as the meaning of the general plural affix. This was somewhat lower than in our previous experiments, and probably reflects the unusual nature of this redundant plural system for English speakers. Around 58% identified plural as (part of) the meaning of (both) gender-specific plural affixes, with many instead identifying only the animacy meanings (i.e., they reported that the gender-specific plural affixes meant "person" or "object")-while 53% interpreted animacy as part of the meaning of the two gender-specific markers, only 36% of participants identified both the animacy and plural meanings together in the same markers. 22 Of course, descriptions of (or failures to correctly describe) an unfamiliar system are not necessarily meaningful. That is, they do not necessarily tell us that participants failed to represent the meanings as plurals. However, it suggests the possibility that at least some participants may have reinterpreted the gender-specific plural as a gender marker at test. If participants are reinterpreting the gender-specific plural as a gender marker, then these results simply replicate those of Study 1. For those participants who do in fact retain the intended meaning of the markers (perhaps despite their problem with describing the system), then our results suggest a preference for gender or gender-conditioned information to be closer to the stem in a double plural system. 23 This supports the idea that the representation of number may depend on whether or not it encodes gender information or is conditioned by it. Importantly, these results also suggest that the ordering preferences we found in Study 1 were not driven by just a preference for ordering derivational morphemes closer to the stem than inflectional morphemes. We discuss both of these points in more detail below.

4 General Discussion

In this article, we started with the observation that although morphological systems vary along many dimensions, there are nevertheless a number of apparent regularities. In the domain of gender systems, for example, there are common semantic bases of classification, and regularities in the interaction with number morphology. Specifically, gender and number are often realised via cumulative exponence, and in the relatively rare cases where they are not, morphemes encoding gender are closer to the noun stem than morphemes encoding number. These regularities have influenced theories of the morphosyntactic representation of gender. For example, split models argue that gender is represented more locally to the noun stem-either within the nominal or nominalising head itself (e.g., Kramer, 2015; Kihm et al., 2005; Harris, 1991; Alexiadou, 2004), or in a distinct projection hierarchically dominating the nominal head (e.g., Picallo, 1991; Carminati, 2005; Antón-Méndez et al., 2002; Panagiotidis, 2018). Assuming that linear proximity mirrors local dependencies between morphemes (e.g., Bobaljik, 2012; Embick, 2010), these models predict that when morphemes are linearised, gender will be closest to the noun stem. By contrast, what we have called bundling models argue that gender does not project separately in the morphosyntax from number (e.g., Ritter, 1993; Carstens, 2003). These models don't make any predictions about the relative order of gender and number (see however, section 4.2), rather they more naturally capture the trend for cumulative exponence. In stark contrast with these models, alternative accounts of morphological ordering and fusion are based not on the nature of hierarchical representations per se, but on distributional information (Hahn et al., 2021; Rathi et al., 2022; Hay and Plag, 2004; Ryan, 2010). Under these accounts, for example, co-occurrence frequencies between morphemes would explain the kinds of regularities noted above.

Across two sets of experiments, here we used artificial language learning methods to test whether learners trained on a novel system of gender and number would exhibit a preference to order gender-encoding morphemes closer to the stem than (exclusively) number-encoding morphemes. Crucially, our experiments were designed so that participants had either no, or minimal information in the input that they could use to determine order. Thus generally, we were interested in whether a mental representation of gender as more local to the noun than number would determine the order they used. In Study 1, we tested English, Italian, and Kîîtharaka speakers on a system with two gender and two number values. For each feature, one value was marked overtly and the other was not, and we held out meanings where both overt morphemes co-occurred. For English-and Italianspeaking participants, we designed systems which balanced the frequency of co-occurrence of all stem+morpheme combinations. For Kîîtharaka-speaking participants, we designed a system where stems were always marked for their particular gender (more similar to natural languages). We found a strong preference to order gender closer to the stem than number in all cases-across all three groups, for both prefixal and suffixal morphemes, for both sex-based (variable) and animacy-based (fixed gender) systems. These results therefore provide strong support that, independent of distributional information, when they are separative, gender is ordered closer to the stem than number.

In Study 2, we explored a somewhat different system, inspired by a natural language phenomenon called double plurality. In these systems, there is a general plural marker than can occur with any stem, and another that is restricted-for example, to stems with a particular gender. We created an artificial language modelling this kind of system, and found a preference in English-speaking learners to place gender-specific number markers (i.e., number markers that encode gender) closer to the stem than general number markers (i.e., markers that encode exclusively number). These results replicate the preference for gender or gender-conditioned information to be most local to the stem, as observed in the first study, but now within a double plural system. It is important to note, however, that these findings do not definitively reveal whether the effects pertain specifically to the representation of gender itself or to locality constraints in allomorphy. It is possible that gender and gender-specific plurals are represented at different levels of the structure, with the lower number feature being projected above gender yet remaining sufficiently local to be conditioned by it. Nonetheless, we can conclude that the projection of gender and/or gender-conditioned features occurs before the projection of the general plural.

4.1 The Derivation/Inflection Divide

Before we turn to the implications of our results for theories of gender specifically, and morpheme order more generally, we first discuss a potential question about what drives participants' preferences in our experiments. In particular, one potential concern in interpreting the overwhelming preference for gender-closest orders in Study 1 is whether participants interpreted gender morphology as derivational and number morphology as inflectional. If this were the case, the observed preference could reflect the more general cross-linguistic tendency to place derivational morphology closer to the root than inflectional morphology. This is problematic since English and Italian both follow this tendency, and they both have derivational morphemes that can be used to express gender (e.g., English 'lion-s/lion-esses' and Italian 'leon-i/leon-ess-e'). Participants' preferences could thus simply reflect L1 knowledge. Even aside from this, distinguishing between a derivational and inflectional interpretation is difficult, and more so in a miniature language (e.g., Dressler and Doleschal, 1990).

However, several aspects of our findings suggest that the derivational flavour of gender (either in general, or for our participants) cannot explain our results. First, in Study 1 we observed the same strong preference for gender-closest orders across all populations we tested. This includes Kîîtharaka speakers, who have no sex-based derivational gender, and no evidence for the relative order of gender and number separately through derivation and inflection in the nominal domain. Further, if anything, we found that the preference for gender-closest orders was slightly weaker in sex-based (variable) compared to animacybased (fixed) systems. If participants were interpreting gender as derivational and number as inflectional, we would expect to see the opposite. Finally, the results from Study 2 show that even when gender information is encoded in a clearly inflectional number morpheme, the preference persists. Even if some participants did reanalyse the gender-specific number marker as a gender marker at test, it is unlikely that this morpheme would be interpreted as derivational given that the referent of the stem alone and the stem with the (reanalysed) gender marker are exactly the same. Setting this issue aside then, we turn to the implications of our results on theories of the morphosyntactic representation of gender.

4.2 Implications for Theories of Gender

The results of Study 1 suggest that mental representations of gender and number may impact morpheme ordering preferences. Specifically, our results support theories in which gender is represented more locally to the nominal stem than number. These results are in line with previous work using artificial language learning methods to provide evidence linking mental representations of syntax and morphosyntax to preferences for particular linearisation patterns (Maldonado et al., 2020; Saldana et al., 2021; Mansfield et al., 2022; Martin et al., 2020 Martin et al., , 2024;; Herce et al., 2023; Saldana et al., 2019). In terms of the spe-cific theories of gender discussed above, our results most naturally align with theories adhering to a split model where gender projects separately and lower than number (e.g., Alexiadou, 2004; Kramer, 2015; Harris, 1991; Panagiotidis, 2018). 24 Our results are less straightforwardly captured by theories which bundle together gender and number features in the morphosyntax (e.g., Ritter, 1993; Carstens, 2003); it is also worth noting that earlier theories have in some cases been revised to reflect split representations (e.g., Carstens, 2024). If we assume that linear proximity mirrors local structural relationships between morphemes, and gender and number are represented and projected together, we would expect to observe more variation in the ordering of separative gender and number morphology in our experiments-and potentially no preference at all. In order to account for the clear preference we in fact found, bundling models would require some further ad hoc ordering mechanism forcing number to linearise outside of gender despite being bundled together (for an example of this, see Ritter, 1993). The cognitive bias found in our experiments could then be argued to reflect this ad hoc mechanism. However, given that the assumption that linear proximity mirrors local structural relationships represented in speakers' minds is well documented in the experimental literature (e.g., Saldana et al., 2021; Maldonado et al., 2020; Martin et al., 2024; Culbertson and Adger, 2014), the most parsimonious interpretation of our results is that they further support it, specially, without a clear definition of the nature of the ad hoc mechanism.

In addition to testing the different predictions of split and bundling models of gender, we also explored potential differences between fixed and variable gender systems. Specifically, we compared an animacy-based system in which stems were shared idiosyncratically across classes, or not shared at all, with a sex-based system in which stems expressed a consistent meaning (female vs. male) across classes. Several formal theories assume that variable gender projects higher than fixed gender, either together with number (e.g., Carminati, 2005; De Vincenzi, 1999) or separate from number (e.g., Panagiotidis, 2018). In these theories, fixed gender is considered to be part of the nominal(ising) head or part of the lexical entry, in contrast to variable gender.

In Study 1, we found a slightly higher preference-although still very low-for alternative number-closest orders in sex-based systems. In our preregistered initial statistical models, which separately analysed data from the experiments with the English and Italian populations, we found stronger evidence for this preference for our Italian-speaking population. However, when we analysed the combined results, we found moderate support for a lower preference for gender-closest orders in sex-based systems across both linguistic populations. While these results are in line with the aforementioned predictions, the overwhelming preference for gender-closest orders suggests that if there is indeed a difference, it is quite weak.

Turning to Study 2, participants' preference for placing gender-specific plural markers closer to the stem than general plural markers is consistent with the idea that number morphology can potentially occupy two different loci. As argued by Kramer (2016a), for example, number morphology which encodes or is conditioned by gender information may be more local (and therefore linearly closer) to the stem than general grammatical number morphology. This mirrors the tendency in natural language double plural systems such as those found in Kinshasa Lingala or Amharic (Di Garbo, 2014; Kramer, 2016a; Acquaviva, 2008; Alexiadou, 2004). In light of this, the results of Study 1 can be seen as specific to the highest projection of number (e.g., NumP). The results of Study 2 would potentially be compatible with the idea that bundling of gender and number might also occur in the morphosyntax, but it could represent a distinct, and lower, projection of number information (Acquaviva, 2008; Alexiadou, 2004).

It is worth noting that here we have focused on plural number, and our results may not generalise to the representation of other number values. For example, some theories consider dual and paucal to be distinct from plural and project lower (evidence for this is also provided by the co-occurrence of dual and plural, with dual loser to the stem in languages like Koasati (Muskogean); Acquaviva, 2008). With these proposals in mind, it would be interesting to test in future work whether the observed effects in our experiment are specific to plural number or are generalisable to dual and/or paucal and shed further light on whether plural and minor number values indeed project in different locations (Acquaviva, 2008; Mathieu, 2014).

4.3 Cognitive and Distributional Biases in Morpheme Ordering

Above, we have argued that participants' robust preference for placing gender closer to the stem than number reflects their mental representations of gender and number. Specifically, we have argued that the meaning and function of gender and number lead to different dependency relations with the stem, represented in a morphosyntactic hierarchy (see also, e.g., Saldana et al., 2021; Maldonado et al., 2020; Bybee, 1985; Embick, 2010). This finding is in line with previous research, especially Saldana et al. (2021) and Culbertson et al. (2020), who highlight the role of meaning in driving ordering preferences for number and case morphology, and nominal modifiers respectively. Here we have focused on very specific theoretical accounts that are in principle independent of these previous findings. However, it is worth emphasising that we are not endorsing a particular view of the origin of these representations. For example, they could reflect innate linguistic representations, or they could reflect learned representations, e.g., about how concepts or meanings are constructed (e.g., Culbertson et al., 2020).

In addition to these representations, whatever their ultimate origin, we also found some evidence that morpheme order preferences are impacted by dependency relations based on co-occurrence statistics (Hahn et al., 2022; Hay and Plag, 2004; Ryan, 2010). Study 1 provides evidence that meaning and function drive sufficiently strong preferences, and that adding evidence from co-occurrence statistics does not make a difference. In particular, in our experiment with Kîîtharaka speakers, stems were not shared across classes, and thus each stem always occurred marked with its gender (in the marked gender class). By contrast, in the experiments with Italian and English speakers, stems were shared, cooccurrence statistics were balanced. Nevertheless, the preference for gender-closest order was equally strong across all three experiments. However, in Study 2, there is more variability in participant's response-i.e., the preference for gender-closest order was not at ceiling. Here, participants saw a subset of stems for which the co-occurrence statistics between morphemes was balanced (unrestricted stems), and a subset where mutual information between the stem and the gender-specific plural marker was higher (restricted stems). This stronger statistical dependency effected participants' behaviour: it led to a stronger preference for placing the gender-specific plural marker closer to the stem than the general plural marker (see figure 4). These results suggest that participants' representation of dependency relations between morphemes can be affected both by their meaning and function as well as by co-occurrence statistics (see also Saldana et al., 2021). 25

4.4 Returning to the Typology

A major aim of the studies reported here was to link individual-level cognitive representations and mechanisms to cross-linguistic tendencies in morpheme order (following previous recent research, e.g., Maldonado et al., 2020; Saldana et al., 2021; Mansfield et al., 2022; Hahn et al., 2022). In this particular case, we focused on the tendency for gender to surface closer to the stem than number when a language has separative morphology for these two categories (e.g., Fuchs et al., 2015). However, we also noted that separative or partially separative expressions of gender and number are very rare (see 2). Even within these rare cases, there are examples of languages which allow both gender-closest and number closest orders. Similarly, while we have not come across a description of double plural system in which a general plural is placed closer to the stem than a gender-restricted plural, the evidence is again very scarce (Kramer, 2016a; Di Garbo, 2014). Thus the tendency for separative morphology to conform to gender-closest orders is not absolute and the typological evidence alone does not allow us to robustly assess the strength of this tendency. For these reasons, experimental methods like artificial language learning can offer a crucial source of additional evidence. These experiments complement natural language data and allow us to make claims about the causal link between human cognition and typology. Biases in representations, like the ones we have uncovered here have the potential to shape languages at each generation, shaping how languages change over time (Bickel, 2015; Smith, 2018; Reali and Griffiths, 2009; Blythe and Croft, 2021; Thompson et al., 2016; Kirby et al., 2015).

Of course, the strong preference that we observe in language learners to place gender information closer to the stem than number information leaves the pervasiveness of cumulative gender-number marking in natural languages unexplained. One possibility is that the tendency for gender and number to be cumulative can be better accounted for by the way in which grammatical gender systems are likely to emerge.

The emergence of grammatical gender systems is a long studied phenomenon and the literature is too vast to discuss it in detail here (Aikhenvald, 2016; Greenberg, 1978; Fodor, 1959; Royen, 1929; Nichols, 1992; Di Garbo, 2014; Corbett, 1991; Matasović, 2004; Bopp, 1816; Luraghi, 2011; Seifart, 2005; Di Garbo and Miestamo, 2019). For the purposes of this brief discussion, it suffices to say that there are two main scenarios. In one scenario, gender systems originate from classifiers and classificatory nouns that grammaticalise into agreement markers and, eventually, form the basis of gender markers on nouns as well (e.g., Greenberg, 1978; Corbett, 1991). In an alternative scenario the development of agreement markers precedes the development of any classificatory distinctions (Nichols, 1992). Greenberg (1978) proposed that gender agreement markers develop from demonstratives and then articles (see also Corbett, 1991). Crucially, the demonstratives must either have marked gender distinctions or their distribution should at least be based on a (covert) gender distinction (e.g., having its use restricted to a particular set of nouns). The articles that develop from these demonstratives (and potentially from succeeding anaphoric pronouns; Corbett, 1991; Greenberg, 1978) begin as definite articles, but later expand to include non-definite determination, and finally become noun markers without any connection to specificity or definiteness. Within his theory, however, the development of such classifying demonstratives in the first place still requires explanation. Greenberg (1978) proposes that classifying demonstratives could develop from classifiers, and from numeral classifiers in particular. In a similar proposal Corbett (1991) highlights the role of classifiers, arguing that the ultimate source of gender systems is nouns with classificatory possibilities (see also Heine and Vossen, 1983; Di Garbo and Miestamo, 2019) which later develop into classifiers before potentially giving rise to demonstratives.

These explanations of the rise of gender thus depend on a transition period between a classifier systems and a gender system. However, Nichols (1992) notes that classifiers and gender do not tend to overlap (for further supporting evidence with larger linguistic coverage, see Grambank, Skirgård et al., 2023, in particular, features GB038, GB057, GB051-53, GB057-58, GB172, GB321). Nichols (1992) instead proposes an alternative scenario whereby classificatory distinctions infiltrate preexisting person and/or number agreement patterns whose distribution might be based on morphologically covert (i.e., not overtly realised) distinctions according to "highly cognitively salient" domains such as animacy or perceived biological sex in animate entities. In this scenario, there are three prerequisites for grammatical gender to arise: a covert system of gender distinctions, and a potentially recruitable formal distinction and preexisting agreement patterns. Thus contrary to the proposals of Greenberg (1978) and Corbett (1991), in the mechanism proposed by Nichols (1992), agreement triggers noun classification (rather than vice versa).

Whichever the scenario, all accounts assume that in its origin, a gender system encroaches on lexical or morphological material where number distinctions are already present, and the succeeding forms that evolve into gender marking will most likely also carry the number features along with them. In the classification-before-agreement scenario (Greenberg, 1978; Corbett, 1991; Heine and Vossen, 1983), gender potentially develops from demonstratives, which would already have distinctions based on number. In the agreement-before-classification scenario (Nichols, 1992), a system of number agreementtogether or not with a system of person agreement-is a prerequisite and classification will be built on the available formal marking in such an agreement system. Across these scenarios, cumulative marking is thus in some sense the default. The most likely route for gender and number to become (or at least be able to be described as) separative is if an initial cumulative gender-number marker can be reanalysed as separative once gender and number agreement systems are in place (as is the case in the later development of already stable gender systems in some Romance languages, e.g., from Latin to Spanish). Alternatively, as observed in Kinshasa Lingala (see 8; Di Garbo, 2014; Bokamba, 1977), a plural class marker can be reanalysed as a general plural, which is placed together with other plural class markers resulting in redundant number marking. In this case, the general plural has lost its gender function and can thus be described as a separative number marker. In the future, plural class markers which frequently co-occur with the general plural could be reanalysed as separative gender morphology-just as some of the participants in our Study 2 appear to have done.

5 Conclusion

In the studies reported here, we tested a hypothesis based on cross-linguistic data and theories of morphosyntax predicting that morphemes encoding gender should be placed closer to the stem than morphemes encoding number. In a series of artificial language learning experiments, we found clear evidence supporting this prediction, across a number of different types of systems, regardless of whether morphemes were prefixal or suffixal, and with equal strength independent of participants' L1. We interpret this result as providing support for theories of gender which treat this morphosyntactic feature as representationally distinct from number, and locally (hierarchically) closer to the nominal stem. Importantly, the ordering preference we found was based on the meaning and function of gender and not on distributional information about the frequency of co-occurrence in the languages participants were trained on. However, we also found some evidence that when learners' preferences were weaker-when gender information was itself encoded in a redundant plural marker-co-occurrence statistics did influence order. These findings shed light on the general mechanisms driving ordering preferences, and add to the growing body of research using artificial language learning experiments to link human cognition to cross-linguistic regularities in language structure.

It is worth noting that in Study 2, the testing block with unrestricted stems always preceded the block with restricted stems. Our results might reflect this to some extent: participants' responses might have become less variable over time, and participants' weak bias towards placing gender information closer to the stem might have become more categorical over time (i.e., eventually they chose their preferred form each time).
